defectClasses.name: Silent truncation
defectClasses.explanation: The tool quietly returns fewer items than you asked for, without saying anything was left out.
defectClasses.example: You ask for 101 refunds per page and get exactly 100 back with no error, so one refund is silently missing.

defectClasses.name: Silent coercion
defectClasses.explanation: The tool quietly changes a value or its type, such as sending a number as text or dropping a setting you sent.
defectClasses.example: A headcount documented as a whole number arrives as the text "1234".

defectClasses.name: Unit mismatch
defectClasses.explanation: The tool reads or reports money in a different unit than its docs say, such as dollars instead of cents.
defectClasses.example: You refund 1234 meaning $12.34, and the tool treats it as $1,234.

defectClasses.name: Undocumented setting
defectClasses.explanation: The tool reacts to a setting its docs never mention, or ignores the documented rules for one.
defectClasses.example: Asking the identify endpoint for an enrich-only field group returns data instead of the documented 400 error.

defectClasses.name: Delayed visibility
defectClasses.explanation: A change you just made takes a while to show up when you read the data back.
defectClasses.example: A refund created a moment ago is missing from the payment's refund list for a few seconds.

defectClasses.name: Duplicate on retry
defectClasses.explanation: Sending the same request again, for example after a timeout, can make the action happen twice.
defectClasses.example: Retrying a refund that timed out creates a second refund for the same payment.

defectClasses.name: Rate limit
defectClasses.explanation: The tool starts refusing requests when too many arrive in a short time.
defectClasses.example: A quick burst of balance checks starts getting status 429 (too many requests).

defectClasses.name: Expiry
defectClasses.explanation: Something the tool gave you stops working after a while, such as a link, a token or a cached answer.
defectClasses.example: A payment link that worked an hour ago now returns an error.

defectClasses.name: Mislabelled meaning
defectClasses.explanation: A field or status means something different from what its name or the docs suggest.
defectClasses.example: A field named employee count range holds a single number instead of a range like 51-200.

defectClasses.name: Honored
defectClasses.explanation: The tool behaves exactly as its docs say.
defectClasses.example: Asking for 101 refunds per page is refused with an error, just as documented.

guardKinds.name: Fix the value
guardKinds.explanation: Before the call, Notary rewrites a value so the tool receives what it really expects.
guardKinds.example: If the tool turns out to read refund amounts 100 times too large, Notary divides the amount by 100 before sending it.

guardKinds.name: Always send the setting
guardKinds.explanation: Notary always fills in a setting the tool needs with a known safe value instead of trusting the tool's default.
guardKinds.example: Every company enrichment call is sent with the basic info, headcount and funding field groups listed.

guardKinds.name: Check first
guardKinds.explanation: Before a money action, Notary reads the current state and stops if the action would repeat or clash with something already there.
guardKinds.example: Before refunding, Notary lists all of the customer's refunds and stops if one already exists for that payment.

guardKinds.name: Careful retries
guardKinds.explanation: Notary never blindly repeats a write, and after a timeout it reads back first and retries only if the write clearly did not happen.
guardKinds.example: A refund call times out, Notary reads back and finds the refund already exists, so it does not send it again.

guardKinds.name: Read every page
guardKinds.explanation: Notary keeps fetching pages until an empty one comes back, so nothing is cut off.
guardKinds.example: To find existing refunds, Notary reads pages of 100 until a page comes back empty.

guardKinds.name: Refuse
guardKinds.explanation: Notary refuses the call outright because no safe fix is known, and the item is held for a person.
guardKinds.example: If a wallet balance arrives in an unexpected form, wallet credits are refused and held for review.

beliefStatuses.name: Hypothesis
beliefStatuses.explanation: Notary has an idea about this promise but not enough evidence yet either way.
beliefStatuses.example: After one test, Notary suspects the page limit is not enforced but needs more tests to be sure.

beliefStatuses.name: Candidate
beliefStatuses.explanation: At least two independent tests strongly agree, and the result is waiting for a reviewer to check it.
beliefStatuses.example: Two different tests both show refund amounts read back unchanged, so the belief waits for review.

beliefStatuses.name: Notarized
beliefStatuses.explanation: A reviewer checked the raw test records and agreed, so Notary now trusts this belief and may act on it.
beliefStatuses.example: The reviewer upholds that refund amounts are in cents, so refunds that depend on it may go through.

beliefStatuses.name: Refuted
beliefStatuses.explanation: The evidence went against this belief, so Notary does not rely on it.
beliefStatuses.example: An idea that balances arrive as text is ruled out when every test returns a whole number.

beliefStatuses.name: Abstained
beliefStatuses.explanation: Notary ran out of test budget before the evidence was clear, so it makes no call either way.
beliefStatuses.example: After five tests the results still point both ways, so actions that need this promise are held.

beliefStatuses.name: Unlearned
beliefStatuses.explanation: Something Notary had trusted stopped matching new evidence, so it withdrew that trust and retired the guards built on it.
beliefStatuses.example: After the tool changes how it pages results, the old page-limit belief is unlearned and its guard is switched off.

decisionStatuses.name: Executed
decisionStatuses.explanation: Notary carried out the action, such as a refund or a plan change, through its guards.
decisionStatuses.example: A refund for a small self-serve customer is sent to Dodo and succeeds.

decisionStatuses.name: Held
decisionStatuses.explanation: Notary paused the action for a person because something it needed was not proven safe yet.
decisionStatuses.example: A refund waits for review because the belief about refund units is not notarized yet.

decisionStatuses.name: Escalated
decisionStatuses.explanation: The billing policy says a person must decide this request, so Notary passed it on.
decisionStatuses.example: A contract customer asks for a full refund, so the account manager decides.

decisionStatuses.name: Denied
decisionStatuses.explanation: Notary turned the request down because the billing policy says no or the money was already returned.
decisionStatuses.example: A refund request for a payment that already has a refund is denied.

probeVerdicts.name: Confirmed
probeVerdicts.explanation: The test result matched exactly one of the competing explanations and ruled out all the others.
probeVerdicts.example: Asking for 101 items returns exactly 100, which only the silent truncation explanation predicted.

probeVerdicts.name: Refuted
probeVerdicts.explanation: The test result went against the explanations being tested.
probeVerdicts.example: Every explanation expected an error or a short page, but the tool returned a normal full page.

probeVerdicts.name: Inconclusive
probeVerdicts.explanation: The test result fit more than one explanation, so it cannot pick between them.
probeVerdicts.example: A request is rejected with an error, which both the honored and the strict-limit explanations predicted.

probeVerdicts.name: Uninformative
probeVerdicts.explanation: The test saw nothing useful, such as an empty list or a missing field, so it says nothing about the promise.
probeVerdicts.example: The test account has only 3 refunds, so a page limit of 100 cannot be tested.

probeVerdicts.name: Invalid
probeVerdicts.explanation: The comparison run read the same as the real run where the two should differ, so the test itself did not work.
probeVerdicts.example: Two different amounts were sent but both read back the same, so the read-back does not reflect what was sent.

policyOutcomes.name: Approve
policyOutcomes.explanation: The billing policy allows the request as asked.
policyOutcomes.example: A small self-serve customer asks for part of a payment back and gets the amount asked.

policyOutcomes.name: Partial
policyOutcomes.explanation: The billing policy allows only part of the request.
policyOutcomes.example: A small business on the growth plan asks for a full refund and gets half the payment back.

policyOutcomes.name: Deny
policyOutcomes.explanation: The billing policy does not allow the request.
policyOutcomes.example: A starter-plan customer asks for a goodwill credit and is offered a refund instead.

policyOutcomes.name: Escalate
policyOutcomes.explanation: The billing policy says a person must decide.
policyOutcomes.example: A customer whose company could not be verified asks for a refund, so a person reviews it.

probeTemplates.name: Edge test
probeTemplates.explanation: Try values at and just past a documented limit to see whether the limit is really enforced.
probeTemplates.example: Ask for 1, 100 and 101 refunds per page and compare what comes back.

probeTemplates.name: Amount round trip
probeTemplates.explanation: Send a known amount and read it back to see whether the tool kept the same unit.
probeTemplates.example: Create a product priced 1234 and check that it reads back as 1234, not 123400.

probeTemplates.name: Repeat a write
probeTemplates.explanation: Send the same write two or three times, as a client would after a timeout, then count how many records exist.
probeTemplates.example: Send the same keyed wallet credit three times and check that the ledger holds one entry.

probeTemplates.name: Count two ways
probeTemplates.explanation: List the same items page by page and all at once, then check that both ways give the same set.
probeTemplates.example: Walk several small pages of payments and compare them with one big page of the same payments.

probeTemplates.name: Write, then read
probeTemplates.explanation: Make a change, then read it back right away and again later to see when it shows up.
probeTemplates.example: Issue a refund, then check the payment's refund list at once, after 1 second and after 3 seconds.

probeTemplates.name: Unknown setting
probeTemplates.explanation: Send a request with a setting the tool should not accept and see whether it is rejected, ignored or used.
probeTemplates.example: Ask the identify endpoint for the headcount field group, which the docs say only enrich supports.

probeTemplates.name: Type edge
probeTemplates.explanation: Read a field where unusual values are likely, such as very large numbers, and check its type matches the docs.
probeTemplates.example: Check that a large company's headcount still arrives as a whole number, not as text.

probeTemplates.name: Small burst
probeTemplates.explanation: Send a short, capped burst of free read-only requests to see whether a rate limit kicks in.
probeTemplates.example: Check the credit balance a few times in quick succession and watch for status 429.
